transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-02
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jon Ruiz (Redwood SE), Aisha Patel (CTO), Marco Santos (Head of ML), Emily Zhao (Infra)

Summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
Redwood and Lynx align on POC scope: measure TTFT (time to first token) and TPOT (time per token) across several model variants and quantization profiles. Primary success metric is interactive TTFT p95/p99 for command parsing workflow; secondary metrics are steady-state throughput (qps) and TPOT for streaming scenarios. Plan: baseline tests, private env runs, shadow traffic, and tuned benchmarks over a 6-week POC.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining — quick intros?
[00:08] Aisha: hi I'm Aisha, CTO at Lynx, i look after platform and product decisions.
[00:13] Marco: Marco here, head of ML, i'll own model evaluation and POC success criteria.
[00:17] Emily: Emily infra — i'll provision the staging and handle access.
[00:21] Maya: thanks. Jon, do you want to kick off on how we normally define latency SLOs?
[00:28] Jon: sure. so we typically split latency into two measures: TTFT, time to first token — that's what humans feel for interactivity — and TPOT, time per output token, which matters for streaming or long responses. both matter but for command-and-control low TTFT is higher priority.
[00:46] Marco: can you give concrete numbers you usually target? we need p95/p99.
[00:50] Jon: yeah, ballpark for interactive workloads we've seen p95 TTFT in the 120–250ms range and p99 around 300–500ms depending on model size and infra. TPOT targets vary — for token streaming we aim p95 < 40–80ms per token for smooth UX. but these depend on seq len, batch, and quantization.
[01:10] Aisha: our product constraint: robot telem commands must start executing within 250ms 95% of the time; edge cases 99% should be under 500ms. If we miss that we can't use hosted variants.
[01:22] Maya: got it — so p95 TTFT <= 250ms, p99 <= 500ms as initial ask; is that correct?
[01:27] Aisha: yes.
[01:28] Jon: good. followups — what qps and burst patterns are you seeing?
[01:33] Marco: steady state about 120 qps for the telemetry NLU route, with 5–10% spikes up to 800–1,000 qps during fleet restarts or OTA rolls. average seq len 32–96, tail up to 512 for diagnostic queries.
[01:46] Jon: okay that's helpful — for 120 qps steady, batching helps cost but increases TTFT. so in the POC we should measure both single-request (batch=1) and small-batch paths (batch 4–8) with and without KV cache.
[02:00] Emily: our infra preference is private deployment in our AWS account (VPC), initially staging, later examine Dedicated. security questions later.
[02:08] Maya: that's fine. for the POC Redwood can either run tests from hosted or deploy our SE runner into staging VPC. which do you prefer?
[02:16] Emily: staging VPC access please — we want the numbers to reflect network egress and NAT latencies.
[02:21] Jon: perfect. we'll need service account and keys.
[02:24] Marco: on measurement, we want p95/p99 for TTFT and TPOT reported per route and per model variant. also histograms over 5-minute windows so we can see spikes.
[02:34] Jon: agreed. recommended measurement plan: 1) synthetic load with loadgen reproducing your trace distribution; 2) production shadowing for a day to capture real tail behavior; 3) microbenchmarks at seq len 64 and 512, batch sizes 1 & 8, quantization int8/int4 and fp16; 4) prefix/KV caching toggles.
[02:51] Aisha: i'd like to see a clear pass/fail matrix: TTFT p95/p99 thresholds, TPOT thresholds, and throughput stability (no more than X% CPU/GPU saturation).
[03:00] Jon: we can make that. proposed pass/fail for the POC: TTFT p95 <= 250ms (PASS), p99 <= 500ms (PASS); TPOT p95 <= 70ms per token for streaming responses (soft pass); steady-state qps >= 110 with <70% GPU utilization (PASS).
[03:16] Marco: what about cold start and KV warm caches? those matter in production.
[03:19] Jon: we'll run cold start tests (container cold) and warmed KV cache tests; measure TTFT delta. include cache hit rates in the report.
[03:27] Maya: timeline — what's realistic?
[03:29] Jon: we typically do a 4–6 week POC. propose 6-week with milestones: week1 kickoffs + infra access + baseline runs; week2 model and harness setup; week3 synthetic load + microbenchmarks; week4 tuning (quant, batching, routing); week5 shadow run; week6 final report and decision meeting.
[03:46] Maya: that aligns with your earlier notes.
[03:49] Aisha: ok good. on tooling — we'll need the benchmark spreadsheet you mentioned and the runner code.
[03:54] Maya: i'll share the spreadsheet and a brief how-to, plus a pointer to the test harness repo.
[03:59] Jon: also recommend tracer ids and distributed tracing so we can map request path and network hop latencies. please attach sample tracing headers.
[04:08] Emily: we can add tracing, SAML is set up but we'll provide a service principal.
[04:12] Marco: on models — we'll evaluate two sizes: 7B opt-like variant and 13B variant; we might try quantized int8 for cost. can Redwood run both fp16 and int8 runs?
[04:22] Jon: yes — our runtime supports fp16, int8 and int4 in many cases; we will surface perf/cost tradeoffs. for small models TTFT is often dominated by kernel launch and request overhead, so batching isn't as beneficial there.
[04:36] Aisha: what's your suggested benchmark matrix so we get apples-to-apples?
[04:40] Jon: suggestion: for each model variant (7B/13B), run seq len 64 and 512, batch sizes [1,4,8], quant profiles [fp16, int8], KV cache on/off. For each cell run 5k requests synthetic with the request size distribution from your traces. Record TTFT p50/p95/p99, TPOT p95, throughput qps, GPU utilization, and cost estimate.
[04:59] Marco: that sounds good. include cold starts (10 container cold starts) and warm state.
[05:05] Jon: yes. we'll also run a 24h shadow traffic run against staging to capture real-world tail.
[05:11] Aisha: any recommended monitoring windows? p99 across 1h or 24h?
[05:15] Jon: measure p95/p99 over 5-minute sliding windows for alerting, and aggregate p95/p99 over the full run for the report — both are useful. for SLO evaluation use rolling 7-day windows once in production, but for POC a 24h shadow is enough.
[05:29] Maya: ok. on decision criteria — if p95/p99 for TTFT pass and throughput is within 10% of your steady requirements, you'll move to Dedicated or private deployment?
[05:38] Aisha: yes, provided the security posture is acceptable. we have SOC2 and KMS requirements and need audit logs.
[05:44] Maya: we'll include compliance docs.
[05:47] Marco: about cost — we want cost per 1k requests estimate for each config. include tokenized cost and infra cost.
[05:53] Jon: we'll produce cost estimates and a recommendation.
[05:56] Emily: one more thing: network egress adds ~20–40ms in our staging — that's why we insisted on testing from our VPC.
[06:03] Jon: noted, we'll run tests from your staging to capture that.
[06:07] Aisha: ok let's recap next steps.
[06:10] Maya: Redwood to share spreadsheet, test harness and proposed runbook by Thursday (2027-11-04). Lynx to share traces and create staging access by Friday (2027-11-05/08). SE to run baseline TTFT tests on 2027-11-09.
[06:25] Marco: agreed. one quick question — what's the recommended granularity for TPOT reporting when responses are variable length?
[06:31] Jon: report TPOT per token and also TPOT normalized to avg response length; provide both median and p95. for streaming UX the p95 per-token is most meaningful.
[06:40] Aisha: thanks everyone, that was helpful.
[06:43] Maya: thank you — we'll follow up with the artifacts and calendar invites.
